§1, §3 opening, our frame

The idea

What harness engineering changes, and the one loop every method shares.

01 · §1

The model stays fixed, the harness learns

TL;DRSelf-improvement can start without touching weights: a loop rewrites the machinery around a frozen model, and the rewritten harness scores higher.

  • Harness code is executable, so a coding agent can search it like an engineer would.
  • Gains land in the harness first; weights can follow later.

Remember: Change what surrounds the model before changing the model.

02 · §3 opening

The ladder of what gets optimized

TL;DRTargets climb a ladder: prompts, context, workflows, harness code, optimizer code, then weights. Higher rungs change more of the system at once.

  • Each rung has methods; the right-hand names are one example each.
  • The post expects near-term gains from the harness-code rung.

Remember: Ask of any method: which rung does it edit?

03 · Our frame

One loop for every method

TL;DREvery method is one loop: select a parent, propose a candidate, run and score it, and let the accept rule decide what the archive keeps.

  • Methods differ in which box they change, not in the loop.
  • The evaluator and permissions belong outside what the loop may edit.

Remember: Find the box a method changes, and you know the method.

§2.1–2.5

Part I · Harness design

How long-running coding agents are built.

04 · §2.1–2.3

Loops, files and sub-agents

TL;DRLong-running agents share three patterns: a goal loop that stops on one metric, files as durable memory, and sub-agents that report back through files.

  • Files survive restarts and context resets; the prompt does not.
  • One scalar metric lets the loop run without a person watching.

Remember: Durable state lives on disk, not in the prompt.

§2.1–2.3 Illustrative
SummaryOpen topic →✓ Understood
05 · §2.4

Anatomy of a coding-agent harness

TL;DRCoding agents converged on one design: context, tools, middleware and a file system around a fixed model. Each part is also something a loop can edit.

  • Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode share this layout.
  • AHE found that editing the system prompt alone can hurt.

Remember: A harness is a set of editable parts around one model.

§2.4 Illustrative
SummaryOpen topic →✓ Understood
06 · §2.5

Harness layer vs core intelligence

TL;DRThe post expects three stages: people build the machinery, the machinery runs auto-research, then stronger models absorb what the harness supplied.

  • Writing harness edits and benefiting from them are different capabilities.
  • Harness gains may be a bridge to better weights, not the end point.

Remember: Today’s harness trick may be tomorrow’s model skill.

§3.1–3.5

Part II · Five families of methods

Each family changes a different box of the loop.

07 · §3.1

Context engineering: curate what the model sees

TL;DRACE and MCE improve what enters the context window, such as a playbook of lessons; Ratchet⁺ retires skills that stop earning their place.

  • Only the context changes; the model and the code stay the same.
  • Rewriting the whole playbook at once can collapse it; small edits do not.

Remember: Better notes, same model.

§3.1 Illustrative
SummaryOpen topic →✓ Understood
08 · §3.2

Workflow design: arrange calls into graphs

TL;DRADAS and AFlow search over workflows, the arrangement of model calls and code, keeping the best-scoring graph.

  • ADAS lets a meta-agent write whole agents as code.
  • AFlow stores workflows in a tree and expands nodes by score plus exploration.

Remember: Structure is searchable, just like words.

§3.2 Illustrative
SummaryOpen topic →✓ Understood
09 · §3.3

A harness that improves itself

TL;DRSTOP, Self-Harness and AHE let a coding agent edit harness code; Gödel Agent⁺ and SICA⁺ edit themselves. Writing edits is easy; benefiting from them is harder.

  • Recursion only helps when the base model is strong enough; weaker models got worse.
  • Held-out tests and small, bounded edits keep changes honest.

Remember: An edit you can write is not yet an edit that helps.

§3.3 Illustrative
SummaryOpen topic →✓ Understood
10 · §3.4

Evolutionary search over agents

TL;DRDGM and AlphaEvolve keep a population and pick parents by score and novelty. HGM⁺ scores parents by their descendants; SIFT⁺ swaps benchmark runs for a pairwise judge.

  • Keeping weak but different agents avoids a dead end.
  • Every child still has to pass the evaluator.

Remember: Keep a tree of tries, not one line of edits.

§3.4 Illustrative
SummaryOpen topic →✓ Understood
11 · §3.5

Harness and weights in one loop

TL;DRSIA, Continual Harness and test-time RL update harness and weights together. Harness-Zero⁺ goes further: it distills the evolved harness into the weights, then drops it.

  • Once weights move, a gain can come from either side, which is harder to credit.
  • Scoring the same signal you train on invites Goodhart effects.

Remember: When weights join the loop, the model is no longer fixed.

§3.5 Illustrative
SummaryOpen topic →✓ Understood

§4 and the appendix

Part III · Limits

Where loops fail, and how far research agents get.

12 · §4

Where the loop still breaks

TL;DRLoops work when a program can score a candidate fast and objectively. Diversity collapse hits Select; reward hacking and overfitting the evolve set hit Evaluate.

  • Proofs beat tests, tests beat judges, judges beat self-assessment (the survey⁺).
  • Keep failed attempts: negative results prune the search.

Remember: The evaluator sets the ceiling.

Benchmarks for auto-research

TL;DRSix appendix benchmarks test research agents end to end. Best reported scores sit at 17–42%, and on RE-Bench humans overtake agents when given more time.

  • Scores are each paper’s own headline; setups differ, so compare within a row.

Remember: Auto-research works on short, checkable tasks first.

Two loops, two speeds

TL;DRA robot harness runs a fast loop every control step; the 12 evolved harnesses add a slow loop that rewrites the harness from rollouts.

§1 · Introduction

1 The big idea

Recursive self-improvement need not start with a model rewriting its weights. It can start in the harness.

§11 quiz question

I. J. Good described an “ultraintelligent machine” that designs better machines. Yudkowsky framed recursive self-improvement as a loop in which an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the machinery that produces it. The post widens the loop: a model can also improve its training pipeline or its deployment system.

That deployment system is the harness: the code around a base model that decides how it plans, calls tools, manages context, stores artifacts and evaluates results. The post argues the harness matters about as much as raw model intelligence, and that the near-term path to self-improvement runs through it.

Our reading frame1 quiz question

A self-improving harness keeps an archive 𝒜 of past versions. It selects a parent, a proposer writes a candidate H′, the base model runs the candidate on tasks, an evaluator scores it, and an accept rule decides what enters the archive. Methods differ only in how they fill these boxes.

Modern harnesses go beyond “LLM plus memory plus tools”. They add workflow design, evaluation, permission controls and persistent state. The post asks for designs that stay simple and generic, like an operating system that hides complex logic behind a small interface.

5 Harness layer vs core intelligence

The post predicts three stages before models rewrite their own weights.

§2.51 quiz question
Step-through

Where improvement lives, stage by stage

Illustrative

Today: people hand-write prompt tricks and harness rules around a fixed model.

Stage 1: harness engineering becomes a meta-methodology. It improves the machinery that produces answers, with fewer heuristic rules and more general mechanisms.

Stage 2: mature harnesses run auto-research and self-improvement loops that help produce smarter models, which in turn need less harness engineering.

Stage 3: harness gains may be internalized into the model, as instruction tuning absorbed prompt tricks. The interface to tools and context remains.

Check yourself

Quiz and flashcards

1.In the last stage, what happens to gains made in the harness?

The post expects stronger core intelligence to absorb what the harness layer once supplied.

§1, §3.1–3.52 quiz questions
Another map

A survey’s grid: what improves, who checks

Beyond the post

Chen et al. (2026) sorted 1,250 arXiv papers from 2024–2026 on two axes. The first asks what the system improves; the four columns below. The second asks who validates the change: a human in the loop, a human on the loop auditing an automatic signal, or nobody (closed loop).

The survey finds almost every paper is human-on-the-loop. Closed loops are rare, and rarest under self-evaluation: a system that rewrites its own definition of “better”. That cell is where bounded self-refinement turns into open-ended recursive self-improvement.

Categories and paper counts from the survey (arXiv 2607.07663). Which column each method on this site falls in is Our reading.

Beyond the post

The same survey ranks improvement signals from strongest to weakest, and finds that how well self-improvement works tracks how high its signal sits.

    One study it cites ran ten rounds of self-critique with no outside check: how much each round changed fell by 55%. A single verification step at round three restored progress.

    Ranking and the ten-round result from Chen et al. (2026). Placing this site’s methods on the rungs is Our reading.

    Selection keeps picking known high-reward parents until the population is variants of one idea.

    Self-check

    9 Check yourself

    Six questions on the whole post.

    Self-check6 quiz questions

    1.Why does the post expect self-improvement to start in the harness rather than in the weights?

    Code is a universal language for systems. Once the harness is code, coding agents can search it like engineers do, while weight updates stay harder to control.

    2.ACE merges delta bullets instead of rewriting the prompt. Which failure does that prevent?

    Whole rewrites tend to compress accumulated knowledge into a short summary. Itemized, deterministic merges keep each bullet.

    3.What did STOP find when it used weaker base models?

    GPT-4 improved its improver; GPT-3.5 and Mixtral got worse. A recursive structure alone is not enough: the base model must be capable enough.

    4.In Self-Harness, when is a proposed edit accepted?

    Validation runs regression tests on both splits. Only edits that fix weaknesses without new failures are merged; rejected edits are logged.

    5.DGM samples parents in proportion to score times 1/(1 + number of children). Why the second factor?

    Favoring members with few children spreads search across the open-ended archive and works against diversity collapse.

    6.Where does the post want evaluators and permission controls to sit?

    A loop optimizes whatever signal it gets. If it can edit the verifier, it can hack the reward. AHE makes those files read-only.

    1. A harness decides how a model plans, acts, remembers and checks. The post argues it matters as much as raw capability.
    2. Optimization targets climbed from prompts to context, workflows, harness code and the optimizer code itself.
    3. Every method is one loop: archive, select, propose, execute, evaluate, accept. They differ in how each box is filled.
    4. Loops work when evaluation is fast and objective. Weak evaluators, reward hacking and diversity collapse remain open.

        Check yourself

        What changed?

        Each question names two methods of the lineage; pick the one change between them.

        1.What is the main change from ADAS to AFlow?

        ADAS shows the meta-agent a flat archive. AFlow stores workflows in a tree and picks the node to expand by mixing score and exploration.

        2.What makes Hyperagents different from DGM?

        DGM’s self-modification procedure is fixed. Hyperagents puts the task agent and the meta agent in one editable program.

        3.Which pair moves from frozen LLMs to training the proposer’s weights?

        ThetaEvolve keeps AlphaEvolve’s program database but trains one small model with RL on its own evolution rollouts.

        4.HGM changes how DGM picks a parent. What does it select by? ⁺

        HGM credits an agent for what its lineage achieves. A high own score does not always mean useful children.

        5.What does Harness-Zero add after evolving a harness? ⁺

        The 9B student scored 44.3% with a minimal harness, above its 41.7% with the evolved harness attached.

        Check yourself

        Tell them apart

        Two questions on what separates methods that look alike.

        1.Which two methods have the same model propose edits to its own harness, with no stronger meta-agent?

        Self-Harness runs the proposer as the same fixed model. STOP’s improver queries the same LM to rewrite itself. Meta-Harness and ADAS use a separate, stronger proposer.

        2.Meta-Harness and GEPA both keep a Pareto set. What does each use it for?

        Meta-Harness returns the accuracy–cost frontier as its result. GEPA samples parents from per-instance winners on its Pareto set.

        3.RRSI builds on AHE. What does it add? ⁺

        Without them, evolution scored 92.8 on the evolve set but only 40.3 out of distribution.

        4.Which change separates SIFT from DGM’s evaluator? ⁺

        The judge compares two agents instead of running the full benchmark, at about $0.011 per comparison.

        The robot harness pipeline

        Every robot harness in your notes is a subset of this pipeline, wrapped around a frozen policy. Tap a part to see what it does and who uses it.

        A robot harness wraps a frozen vision-language-action model (VLA) or world action model (WAM) in perception tools, a planner, primitives, verifier gates, memory and recovery. The policy handles contact; the harness decides what to do next and checks that it worked. Twelve of the 35 papers also add an optimizer: the post’s loop, rewriting the harness from rollouts.

        InteractiveOur synthesis of 35 papers

        How to read this pipeline. Follow the arrows: the goal and the camera feed the planner, the planner hands each subgoal to code, a primitive or the frozen policy, the robot acts, and a gate checks the result. Pass moves on; fail goes to recovery.

        Two loops, two speeds

        The runtime loop runs every control step. The optimization loop is the post’s loop, run across whole rollouts, and only evolved harnesses have it.

        Six harness patterns

        Where the policy sits decides the pattern. Each card opens that pattern in the pipeline explorer on Compare.

        Strongest evidence so farHarnessPAI reaches 96.5% on LIBERO-PRO with π0.5 frozen; fine-tuning π0.5 on the harness’s own successes reaches 73.7%. Zetta lifts π0.5 from 34.5% to 90.8% on the LIBERO-Pro Goal suites. Splits differ, so compare gains within a paper.

        Takeaways

        What to remember

        1. A robot harness wraps a frozen policy in perception, planning, primitives, gates, memory and recovery.
        2. It runs two loops: a runtime loop every control step, and in 12 of 35 papers an optimization loop across rollouts.
        3. The optimization loop is the post’s loop, with a coding agent rewriting robot harness code.
        4. Results use different splits of the same benchmarks, so compare gains within a paper.

        Check yourself

        Tell the patterns apart

        Three questions on what separates the robot harness patterns.

        1.In Harness-VLA, what is the frozen VLA’s role?

        An LLM planner composes analytic primitives (move, grasp, gripper) and calls the frozen VLA only where contact is hard, re-staging and retrying when it fails.

        2.What separates Zetta from Harness-VLA?

        Both keep the VLA frozen. Zetta adds the post’s loop: agents diagnose failure clusters, patch critics and recovery, and keep a patch only if held-out seeds improve.

        3.Across the 35 robot harnesses, which part appears in the fewest papers?

        Memory and verifier gates appear in most robot harnesses. Rehearsal, previewing an action in IK or a planner before committing, appears only in World Action Agent.
